content.overview: Trespass ab initio is the common-law doctrine under which a person who enters lawfully under authority of law and then abuses that authority by committing an act amounting to trespass may be treated retrospectively as a trespasser from the beginning.
content.glance: Trespass ab initio is the common-law doctrine under which a person who enters lawfully under authority of law and then abuses that authority by committing an act amounting to trespass may be treated retrospectively as a trespasser from the beginning.
content.study:
Trespass ab initio is the common-law doctrine under which a person who enters lawfully under authority of law and then abuses that authority by committing an act amounting to trespass may be treated retrospectively as a trespasser from the beginning.

The doctrine is exceptional. A lawful entry does not become tortious merely because of nonfeasance or a later omission; the classic rule requires an affirmative wrongful act that abuses the authority under which the entry was made.

This topic is included as a dedicated Torts coverage unit so students can distinguish the doctrine from neighbouring causes of action and apply it to factual problems.

sections.heading: Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: The doctrine is exceptional. A lawful entry does not become tortious merely because of nonfeasance or a later omission; the classic rule requires an affirmative wrongful act that abuses the authority under which the entry was made.

sections.heading: Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. The defendant initially enters or remains under authority of law or a legally recognised authority. 2. The authority is subsequently abused by an affirmative wrongful act. 3. The later act itself amounts to trespass or an actionable abuse of the authority. 4. Mere failure to perform an obligation is not, by itself, sufficient to invoke the doctrine.
